sections.h2: Can a squatter become the owner of a Utah house?
sections.html:
Only through adverse possession, and Utah makes that hard. The law starts from the presumption that the person holding legal title is the one in possession, and anyone else's occupation is treated as subordinate to that title.

Utah Code 78B-2-208 allows that presumption to be rebutted only by showing the property was held and possessed adversely to the legal title for at least seven years before the action began. A short stay in a vacant house, however unwelcome, does not come close.

sections.h2: What must a Utah adverse possession claim prove?
sections.html:
The claimant must show continuous occupation and a claim of right for seven years, and that taxes on the land were paid. Utah Code 78B-2-214 bars a claim unless the party and the party's predecessors and grantors paid all taxes levied and assessed on the land.

That tax requirement does a lot of work. A person who sneaks into a house and never pays the county cannot meet it. Utah also separates two kinds of claim.

  • Claim under a written instrument or court judgment: seven years of continuous occupation while holding a document that purports to convey title (78B-2-210).
  • Claim with no document: only the land actually occupied counts, and the occupation must be continued, under a claim of title and exclusive of any other right (78B-2-212).

sections.h2: What counts as possession under a written instrument?
sections.html:
Land is treated as possessed if it has been usually cultivated or improved, protected by a substantial enclosure, or used for fuel, fencing timber, husbandry, pasturage or the ordinary use of the occupant. Those tests come from Utah Code 78B-2-211.

The statute also covers a known farm or single lot that is partly improved: the uncleared part is treated as occupied for the same time as the improved part. For lots in a divided tract, possession of one lot is not possession of another lot in the same tract. That limit matters for subdivisions, where a neighbor's use of an extra parcel does not stretch to cover the whole tract.

sections.h2: What is the tax title presumption in Utah?
sections.html:
A person holding a tax title for four years before the lawsuit can be presumed the owner by adverse possession, but the presumption can be rebutted. Utah Code 78B-2-209 says the legal title owner can defeat it by showing they or a predecessor actually occupied or possessed the property under the title, or that the tax title holder failed to pay all taxes assessed during the four years.

This ties squatter law to property tax law. An owner who keeps paying the county bill and keeps visiting the property is hard to displace.

sections.h2: How can an owner remove a trespasser quickly in Utah?
sections.html:
Since May 7, 2025, an owner or authorized agent can ask law enforcement to remove a trespasser immediately by filing a verified complaint, without a lawsuit first. This limited remedy is in Utah Code 78B-6-817.

The owner must attest to all of the following.

  • The trespasser entered unlawfully and remains on the property.
  • The property was not open to the public when the person entered.
  • The owner told the trespasser to leave.
  • The trespasser is not a current or former tenant under a written rental agreement the owner authorized.
  • The trespasser is not an immediate family member.
  • No litigation about the property is pending between the owner and the trespasser.

The complaint is made under penalty of perjury and comes with proof of ownership and identification, or papers showing an agent's authority.

sections.h2: What happens after the complaint is filed?
sections.html:
If the owner appears entitled to relief, law enforcement serves a notice to immediately vacate, either by hand delivery or by posting it, and puts the owner in possession. Officers try to verify the trespasser's identity, and may arrest for trespass, outstanding warrants or another legal cause.

After service, the owner may ask officers to keep the peace while locks are changed and the trespasser's belongings are moved to or near the property line. Neither law enforcement nor the owner is liable for loss or damage to that property unless the removal was wrongful.

sections.h2: What is the risk of using the Utah removal process wrongly?
sections.html:
A person who is wrongfully removed can sue and be restored to possession. They may recover actual costs and damages, statutory damages equal to three times the fair market rent of the dwelling, court costs and reasonable attorney fees, and the court must expedite the case.

The complaint form itself warns that false statements or wrongful use can make the owner liable. That is why the process excludes anyone with a written lease, current or former, and anyone in litigation with the owner. If the occupant claims a lease, or was a tenant, the usual route is the unlawful detainer process in 78B-6-802, which sets the notice periods for tenants who stay past a term, fail to pay rent or breach the lease.

sections.h2: Is squatting also a crime in Utah?
sections.html:
Entering or remaining unlawfully can be criminal trespass. Under Utah Code 76-6-206, a person commits it by remaining unlawfully with intent to cause annoyance, injury or damage, or by remaining on property after notice against entering given by personal communication, fencing or posted signs.

The offense is a class B misdemeanor, and a class A misdemeanor if committed in a dwelling. The owner may also recover statutory damages of three times the resulting damage or $500, whichever is greater, plus attorney fees up to $250 and court costs. Criminal charges are separate from the civil right to recover possession.

sections.h2: How do vacant and inherited houses become squatter targets?
sections.html:
Vacant houses carry the most risk because no one is there to object. Utah law protects the owner who stays involved, which means a few habits go a long way.

  • Pay the property tax bill on time, since adverse possession requires the claimant to have paid.
  • Visit the property and keep notice against entering posted.
  • Tell trespassers in writing to leave and keep a record.
  • Keep proof of ownership ready, such as a recorded deed or letters from probate.

For an inherited house in a probate that has not been opened, ownership paperwork is often the missing piece. A family may need a personal representative before anyone can sign the complaint as owner.

sections.h2: When does selling make more sense than fighting for the house?
sections.html:
Selling can be the practical choice when an owner lives out of state, cannot supervise the property, or does not want to carry insurance and tax on a house that has become a liability. A cash buyer can purchase a house with an occupant problem as is, though the owner should clear possession issues through the legal routes above where possible.

If the house is vacant and the owner simply wants out, the sale does not require repairs or staging. If a trespasser is present, ask an attorney which route fits the facts before listing.

faqs.q: How long does adverse possession take in Utah?
faqs.a: At least seven years of continuous occupation under a claim of right, with all property taxes paid by the claimant and predecessors, under Utah Code 78B-2-208 and 78B-2-214.

faqs.q: Do squatters have rights in Utah?
faqs.a: Not automatically. Utah presumes the title holder is in possession. A squatter would have to prove seven years of continuous adverse possession and tax payment, and an owner may also use the 2025 trespasser removal process.

faqs.q: Can I have a squatter removed without going to court in Utah?
faqs.a: Often yes. Utah Code 78B-6-817 lets an owner file a verified complaint with law enforcement, which can serve a notice to vacate and put the owner in possession, if the six listed conditions are met.

faqs.q: What if the person in my house says they are a tenant?
faqs.a: The removal process excludes current or former tenants under a written rental agreement the owner authorized. A tenancy dispute goes through the unlawful detainer process under Utah Code 78B-6-802 instead.

faqs.q: What happens if I wrongly remove someone in Utah?
faqs.a: The person can sue for restoration of possession, actual damages, statutory damages of three times fair market rent, court costs and attorney fees under Utah Code 78B-6-817(5).
